title: Week 1: What an Experiment in High Energy Physics Is
text:
What high energy physics is
Overview. The first week does not introduce a technique. It sets out what kind of subject this is, what every experiment in it is made of, and why the course covers both collider experiments and experiments buried deep underground. Two sets of material come together: an introduction to particle physics experiments in general, and an introduction to the second half of the course, which covers experiments that do not use a collider. Later weeks take each piece in turn. Week 2 starts with the accelerator, and its two main quantities, beam energy and luminosity, first appear here as the accelerator’s contribution to an experiment.
The running examples are the ones the handouts use: Rutherford’s scattering experiment set beside the CDF experiment at the Tevatron, the LEP ring with its four experiments, and an underground dark matter experiment at SNOLAB.
What is the subject for? The handout gives a plain answer.
The handout adds a view about method. Physics is concerned with the universe we live in, and experiments are how we look at it. On this view, ideas with no connection to experimental observation are not physics. Theory alone belongs with mathematics and philosophy, and experiment alone belongs with engineering and computer science. Physics needs both, and this course is about the experimental side.
The handout sums up a high energy physics experiment in a sentence attributed to D. C. Bailey (circa 1990): “smash things together, see what flies out, figure out what happened.” The next section turns that sentence into a list of parts.

title: Week 1: What an Experiment in High Energy Physics Is
text:
Anatomy of an experiment
What does every particle physics experiment need, from the earliest to the largest?

Definition. The handout lists five parts of what it calls the archetypal particle physics experiment.

The beam is a stream of particles that is aimed at something.
The target is what the beam hits. In a collider it is the other beam.
The detector records what comes out of the collision.
Data acquisition (DAQ) is the electronics and computing that read the detector out and store the data.
Analysis is the work of turning the recorded data into a measurement.

A sixth item, the team of people who do all this, is listed alongside them.

Accelerators, detectors and analysis
The five parts group into three areas of work, each with its own figure of merit. The handout gives a rough share of the effort for each.








Area
Figure of merit
Rough share of the effort




Accelerators and beams
Energy E and luminosity \mathcal{L}
25%


Detectors
Resolution, written \sigma/p
50%


Analysis
Signal to background, S/B
25%



The handout marks the analysis share as the part where theory enters. The subscripts in the resolution entry are hard to read in the scan, so we take \sigma/p to mean the spread of a measured momentum relative to the momentum itself.

Definition. The luminosity \mathcal{L} of a collider is the factor that turns a cross section \sigma (an effective area for a process) into an interaction rate: \text{rate} = \mathcal{L}\,\sigma .

A higher E opens up heavier particles, and a higher \mathcal{L} makes rare processes happen often enough to record. Week 2 works out what limits both.

Definition. The resolution of a detector is how finely it can measure a quantity. For momentum, \sigma/p is the typical size of the measurement error \sigma divided by the momentum p being measured. A smaller number is a better measurement.


Definition. Signal is the kind of event we are looking for, and background is everything else that looks similar enough to be mistaken for it. The ratio S/B says how prominent the signal is against the background.

Every later topic in the course improves one of these three: a better beam, a better detector, or a cleaner separation of signal from background.

text:
Machines and detectors used as examples
Where do the parts sit in a real facility? The handout shows two.

LEP and DELPHI
The LEP ring was an electron-positron collider at CERN. The handout’s layout of its underground structures shows a single ring with four experimental halls, at points 2, 4, 6 and 8, holding the experiments L3, Aleph, Opal and Delphi. The other points around the ring are access points.
The handout also gives cross-sections of the DELPHI detector. Read from the beam pipe outward, the barrel region contains these layers.

  beam and interaction point
  
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
  
  
    vertex detector
    inner detector
    TPC
    barrel RICH
    outer detector
    HPC
    superconducting coil
    scintillator hodoscope
    barrel hadron cal
    muon chambers
  
  Schematic order only, not to scale. Read from the labels on the handout's cross-section.







Note





Figure 2. The barrel layers of DELPHI. Each colour marks a role: green for tracking, purple for particle identification, orange for energy measurement, yellow for the magnet and its scintillator, blue for the muon system.



The layers are ordered by what a particle meets first. Tracking layers close to the beam record where charged particles go. A magnet bends those tracks, which is what lets their momentum be measured. Calorimeters, which absorb particles and measure their energy, sit outside the tracking, and muon chambers form the outermost layer. The handout also labels forward detectors near the beam pipe in each direction, a small angle tagger (SAT), and the superconducting quadrupoles of the machine itself. Each of these systems has a week of its own later in the course, and the acronyms (TPC, RICH, HPC) are defined there.


CDF at the Tevatron
The CDF pages show the same design in a proton-antiproton experiment: a solenoid magnet and tracking chambers in the middle, calorimeters around them, and muon systems on the outside. The cross-section labels a silicon vertex detector and a vertex tracking chamber closest to the interaction point, then a central tracking chamber, the solenoid, and the central electromagnetic and hadron calorimeters. Plug and forward calorimeters cover the regions nearer the beam.
The CDF cross-section marks the extent of its detector regions by a quantity called \eta, with labels at \eta = 0, 0.9, 2.4 and 4.2, and the forward calorimeters at the largest value. The handout does not say what \eta is, so we add it here.

Definition. The pseudorapidity \eta of a direction is \eta = -\ln\tan\frac{\theta}{2}, where \theta is the angle between that direction and the beam axis.

Perpendicular to the beam (\theta = 90^\circ) gives \eta = 0, and directions closer to the beam give larger \eta. The formula is a way to label angles so that detector coverage is easy to state.






Note



Worked example. The three CDF values correspond to these angles from the beam axis, using \theta = 2\arctan(e^{-\eta}):

\eta = 0.9 gives \theta \approx 44^\circ.
\eta = 2.4 gives \theta \approx 10^\circ.
\eta = 4.2 gives \theta \approx 1.7^\circ.

The forward calorimeters therefore look almost straight down the beam pipe.

The non-collider half of the course
The second instructor’s introduction opens with a question: why two professors this term? The slides answer with a pair of pictures. On one side is a collider experiment, ATLAS at the LHC. On the other is SuperCDMS at SNOLAB, which sits 2 km underground. The course is called eHEP on the slides, and the slides then ask whether these are really all High Energy Physics.

Figure 3. The energy attached to each measurement on the slides. The horizontal axis is logarithmic, so each tick is a factor of 1000 in energy.



Each marker refers to a measurement the second half of the course discusses.

125 GeV. A collider measurement: the ATLAS plot shows a bump in a mass spectrum at about 125 GeV, which is the Higgs boson.
Below 10 GeV. The plot for dark matter direct detection has the dark matter particle’s mass on its horizontal axis. Dark matter is invisible matter whose presence is inferred from its gravity, and direct detection tries to catch one of its particles scattering in a detector. The slide’s arrow marks the mass region below about 10 GeV. The candidate particle in this kind of search is a weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP).
About 3 MeV. The plot for neutrinoless double beta decay shows a continuous spectrum for ordinary double beta decay, and marks where a sharp line for the neutrinoless version would appear at the high-energy end, at about 3 MeV in this example.
keV. The plot for coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering (CEvNS) shows a spectrum of nuclear recoil energies that reaches the keV scale. In CEvNS a neutrino scatters from a nucleus as a whole.
eV. The last plot is a phonon energy spectrum at the eV scale, from a detector that reads out vibrations in a crystal.

These short descriptions are for orientation only. The non-collider experiments are described in later weeks, and the slide plots are not reproduced here.


What is shared and what differs
The slide called “So…” places the two kinds of experiment side by side.



Collider experiments want
Underground experiments want

Better energy resolution

Faster detection

Underneath the differences, the slide lists common threads:

particle interaction with materials,
particle identification and signal-background discrimination,
the trigger, data acquisition and event reconstruction.

Those threads are why one course covers both. A detector that measures a 125 GeV photon pair and a detector that measures an eV-scale crystal signal both depend on how particles deposit energy in matter, on telling signal from background, and on reading out and reconstructing events. The second instructor’s part of the course covers three non-collider topics: dark matter direct detection, CEvNS, and neutrinoless double beta decay. title: Week 1: What an Experiment in High Energy Physics Is
text:
Summary






Note



Key takeaways from Week 1:

What the subject is. High energy physics is the discovery and measurement of the fundamental constituents of matter and their basic interactions, and this course is about the experimental side.
Five parts. Every experiment, from Rutherford’s to CDF’s, has a beam, a target, a detector, data acquisition and analysis, run by a team.
Three figures of merit. Accelerators are judged by energy E and luminosity \mathcal{L}, detectors by resolution \sigma/p, and analysis by signal to background S/B.
Detectors are layered. Tracking sits closest to the beam, then particle identification, calorimeters and, outermost, muon chambers, as in DELPHI and CDF.
Two halves, one toolkit. Collider and underground experiments span eV to hundreds of GeV, and they share particle interaction with matter, signal and background discrimination, and trigger and readout.



Next week: Week 2 covers how accelerators bend, focus and accelerate a beam, and what sets the luminosity.

title: Week 2: Accelerator Physics
text:
What a circular accelerator is made of
Overview. A particle accelerator must do three jobs to a beam of charged particles: keep the particles on a closed path, keep them close to that path, and give them energy. The lecture starts with the first two (bending and focusing with magnets), builds the mathematics of a particle wobbling around its ideal path, and uses that to define the luminosity \mathcal{L}, the quantity that sets how often a collider produces an interaction of interest. It then turns to acceleration with radio-frequency fields and to the stability of the energy of the beam. The interaction rate \mathcal{L}\,\sigma (luminosity times cross section) was introduced earlier in the course and is restated below where we need it.
The running example is the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), with the Tevatron as the lecture’s comparison machine. The lecture’s reference text is Edwards and Syphers, An Introduction to the Physics of High Energy Accelerators.
Which pieces of hardware does a ring need? The lecture starts from circular structures and assigns one job to each kind of field.
The rest of the week takes these in turn, then uses them to compute luminosity and to explain why colliders are built at all.

title: Week 2: Accelerator Physics
text:
Bending with a dipole
How strong must a magnetic field be to bend a beam of a given momentum around a ring?

Definition. A dipole magnet produces a uniform field B across the beam. A particle of unit charge and momentum p moves on a circular arc of radius \rho, the bending radius. The product B\rho is the magnetic rigidity of the beam.

A dipole of length \ell deflects the beam by the angle
\theta = \frac{\ell}{\rho}.
The radius follows from balancing the Lorentz force against the curvature, and in the units the lecture uses (momentum in GeV/c, field in tesla, radius in metres) it reads

\rho = \frac{p}{0.3\,B}, \qquad B\rho = \frac{p}{0.3}.

The rigidity is the beam’s momentum expressed as a magnetic quantity: a stiffer beam needs either a larger field or a larger radius.






Note



Worked example. Take a beam with p = 3 GeV/c in a field of B = 1 T. Then \rho = 3/(0.3 \times 1) = 10 m. A magnet of length \ell = 1 m bends this beam by \theta = 1/10 = 0.1 rad. Doubling the momentum at fixed field doubles the radius.

title: Week 2: Accelerator Physics
text:
Focusing with a quadrupole
A dipole bends the reference path but does not stop particles from drifting away from it. What restores them?

Definition. A quadrupole magnet has four poles and a field that vanishes on the axis and grows linearly with distance from it. For a beam travelling along s, the transverse field components are proportional to the displacements: B_x = g\,y, \qquad B_y = g\,x, \qquad g = \frac{\partial B_y}{\partial x}. The constant g is the field gradient.

The field pushes a particle back toward the axis in one transverse plane and away from it in the other. Which plane is which depends on the sign of g and of the particle’s charge. The lecture quotes typical gradients to show how the technology has advanced: about 12 T/m for iron magnets (CESR, a 10 GeV electron ring), about 75 T/m for the superconducting Tevatron (1 TeV), and 223 T/m for the main quadrupoles of the LHC.

Weak and strong focusing
The first designs used a single magnet for both jobs. If the dipole field falls off as B_y = B_0/r^n with 0<n<1, one magnetic structure both bends and focuses. This is weak focusing, and it was the basis of early cyclotrons and of the weak-focusing synchrotrons and betatrons that followed.
Strong focusing separates the jobs and uses the optics of a lens system. A single lens focuses in both planes, but a quadrupole focuses in one plane and defocuses in the other. Recall from optics that a series of alternating focusing (F) and defocusing (D) elements gives net focusing, provided the particle sits, on average, closer to the axis in the D elements than in the F elements. A repeating sequence of focusing, drift, defocusing and drift is called a FODO lattice (the O is the drift space), and its repeating length L is the cell size.

  FODO lattice: trajectory through alternating lenses
  
  
  s
  
    
    
    
  
  
    
    
  
  
  
    FD
    FDF
  
  
  cell size L







Note





Figure 1. The particle is farther from the axis at the focusing lenses than at the defocusing lenses, so the net effect is focusing.





The quadrupole as a thin lens
A quadrupole of length \ell gives a particle at transverse position x a momentum kick proportional to x, and so a change of slope \Delta x' \equiv \theta_x that also grows with x:
\Delta p_x = e\,g\,\ell\,x, \qquad |\Delta x'| \simeq \frac{g\,\ell\,x}{B\rho}.
The optics relation for a thin lens is x' = x/F with F the focal length, so

F \simeq \left(\frac{g\,\ell}{B\rho}\right)^{-1}, \qquad F \propto p .

At fixed gradient, a stiffer beam is focused less strongly. In practice the focal length is about one cell length, F \approx L, and the quadrupole is about a tenth of a cell, \ell \approx L/10. Those two conditions fix the gradient, so the gradient must grow in proportion to the momentum.

title: Week 2: Accelerator Physics
section: Describing motion about the reference orbit
text:
Describing motion about the reference orbit
To design the lattice we need equations for how far a particle strays from the ideal path.

Definition. The reference orbit is the ideal closed path of a particle of the design momentum. Position along it is the arc length s(t). We use a coordinate system that moves with the particle: \hat{s} points along the orbit, \hat{x} points radially (in the bending plane), and \hat{y} points perpendicular to that plane. The transverse position is x\hat{x} + y\hat{y}.

The origin O' of this frame moves at speed u = ds/dt along \hat{s}. Because the frame rotates as it follows the bend, the particle’s velocity in the laboratory picks up a term from the rotation. The result, with \rho the local bending radius, is
\vec{v}_{\text{lab}} = \dot{x}\,\hat{x} + \dot{y}\,\hat{y} + u\left(1+\frac{x}{\rho}\right)\hat{s}.
A particle at larger x (outside the bend) travels a longer path per unit of s, which is the factor 1 + x/\rho. The unit vectors also change along the path: d\hat{x}/dt = (u/\rho)\hat{s}, d\hat{s}/dt = -(u/\rho)\hat{x}, and d\hat{y}/dt = 0. The lecture leaves the resulting expression for the acceleration as an exercise.

The equations of motion
We start from \vec{F} = d\vec{p}/dt = e\,\vec{v}\times\vec{B}. Four steps turn this into equations we can solve:

Magnetic forces do no work, so |\vec{p}| is constant and the term dp/dR vanishes. For a relativistic particle the resulting equation is \ddot{\vec{R}} = (e/p)\,\dot{R}\,(\dot{\vec{R}}\times\vec{B}).
Change the independent variable from time to the path coordinate s, using \dot{y} = y'u and \ddot{y} = y''u^2 + \dot{u}y', where a prime is d/ds.
Keep the two transverse components \hat{x} and \hat{y}, since \hat{s} is less interesting. This gives one equation per plane.
Expand the field for small displacements. The symmetry of a dipole or quadrupole makes several terms vanish (for example B_x(x) = B_x(-x) and B_x(y) = -B_x(-y)), and Maxwell’s equation \nabla\times\vec{B} = 0 ties the two remaining gradients together: \partial B_x/\partial y = \partial B_y/\partial x.

Only one term survives on the reference orbit itself, and it is the dipole relation
\frac{1}{\rho} = \frac{e\,B_y}{p}.
Off the orbit we define the focusing strength

K \equiv \frac{e}{p}\,\frac{\partial B_y}{\partial x}\Big|_0, \qquad \frac{e\,B_y}{p} = \frac{1}{\rho} + K\,x .

and the two equations of motion become
y'' - K\,y = 0, \qquad x'' + \left(K + \frac{1}{\rho^2}\right)x = 0 .
These are linear differential equations whose solutions are periodic in s. The extra 1/\rho^2 in the x equation is the weak focusing that a bend provides on its own. In this convention K>0 focuses in x and defocuses in y.

Which simple regions do we need to describe a whole ring? The lecture considers three cases.



Region
K
1/\rho^2




Dipole

Free (drift) space

Quadrupole

Definition. A transfer matrix M maps a particle’s transverse state (x, x') at one position to its state a distance s downstream: \begin{pmatrix} x \\ x' \end{pmatrix}_s = M \begin{pmatrix} x \\ x' \end{pmatrix}_0 .

In a drift of length s the slope is constant and the position grows linearly:
M_{\text{drift}} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & s \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.
In a quadrupole with K>0 the x motion is focusing and the y motion defocusing:
M_{\text{focus}} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\sqrt{K}s & \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{K}}\sin\sqrt{K}s \\ -\sqrt{K}\sin\sqrt{K}s & \cos\sqrt{K}s \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
M_{\text{defocus}} = \begin{pmatrix} \cosh\sqrt{K}s & \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{K}}\sinh\sqrt{K}s \\ \sqrt{K}\sinh\sqrt{K}s & \cosh\sqrt{K}s \end{pmatrix}.
The oscillating form describes the plane the magnet focuses, and the hyperbolic form the plane it defocuses. Where the dipole term 1/\rho^2 matters, K is replaced by K + 1/\rho^2 in the x matrix.
In the thin-lens limit of the thin-lens relation above the same lens and drift appear as
M_{\text{lens}} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1/f & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad M_{\text{drift}} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & L \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.
Chaining elements is matrix multiplication, with the first element on the right. The lecture’s textbook figure multiplies a defocusing lens, a drift of length L, and a focusing lens of focal length f:
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -\tfrac{1}{f} & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & L \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \tfrac{1}{f} & 1 \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} 1+\tfrac{L}{f} & L \\ -\tfrac{L}{f^2} & 1-\tfrac{L}{f} \end{pmatrix}.






Note



Worked example. Take L = f. The product is \begin{pmatrix} 2 & f \\ -1/f & 0\end{pmatrix}, which has determinant 0 + 1 = 1 as every transfer matrix here must. The lower left entry is -L/f^2 = -1/f, the same as the lower left entry of a single thin focusing lens of focal length f. So the pair focuses even though one of its lenses defocuses. A ray entering at position x_0 with zero slope leaves at position 2x_0 and slope -x_0/f: it is farther from the axis but heading back toward it.


A whole ring is the product of the matrices of all its dipoles, drifts, and quadrupoles. That product is solved numerically to find which lattices give stable orbits.

title: Week 2: Accelerator Physics
text:
Beam envelope and emittance
So far we followed one particle. What describes the whole beam?
Hill’s equation. When the focusing varies around the ring but repeats after one circumference C, each transverse plane obeys
u'' + K(s)\,u = 0, \qquad K(s + C) = K(s),
where u stands for x or y and K has the sign convention that makes it focusing. This is Hill’s equation. The lecture looks for solutions of the form u(s) = a(s)\cos(\phi(s) + \delta), an oscillation whose amplitude and phase both vary with s. Writing the general solution as u(s) = c(s)\,u_0 + v(s)\,u_0' with a cosine-like and a sine-like part, and setting c = w\cos\phi and v = w\sin\phi, one finds
w'' + K\,w = \frac{1}{w^{3}}, \qquad w^2\phi' = 1 .
The lecture asks whether the reader can prove this.

Definition. The Courant-Snyder parameters are \beta(s) = w^2(s), \qquad \alpha(s) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta'(s), \qquad \gamma(s) = \frac{1 + \alpha^2(s)}{\beta(s)} . The function \beta(s) is the betatron function. The phase advances as \phi'(s) = 1/\beta(s), so \phi(s) = \int_0^{s}\frac{ds'}{\beta(s')}.

The equation \phi' = 1/\beta says that where \beta is large the oscillation is slow. The betatron oscillations themselves are the transverse wobbles of particles about the reference orbit.
The particle’s coordinates and slope stay on an ellipse. The lecture leaves as an exercise that the combination

\gamma\,y^2 + 2\alpha\,y\,y' + \beta\,y'^2 = \epsilon

is constant along the orbit. This is the Courant-Snyder invariant. It is an ellipse in (y, y') space, and its enclosed area is \pi\epsilon provided \beta\gamma - \alpha^2 = 1, which holds by the definition of \gamma above.

  Phase-space ellipse of one particle
  
  
  y
  y'
  
  area = pi x epsilon







Note





Figure 2. A particle’s (y, y') point moves around the ellipse of the Courant-Snyder invariant as it passes through the lattice. The shape of the ellipse changes from place to place while its area does not.



Using the invariant, the solution can be written in terms of \epsilon and \beta:

y(s) = \sqrt{\epsilon\,\beta(s)}\,\cos\big(\phi(s) + \delta\big),

with \delta an arbitrary phase. The amplitude \sqrt{\epsilon\beta(s)} is set by two things: the machine, through \beta(s), and the particle, through \epsilon. This is the reason \beta(s) can be interpreted as the beam envelope around the machine. The betatron oscillations occur in both transverse planes, each with its own \beta_x, \epsilon_x and \beta_y, \epsilon_y, and the two are independent to first order.

Definition. The emittance \epsilon measures the size of a beam in transverse phase space, position and slope together. In the lecture’s convention it is the value of the Courant-Snyder invariant. It is constant along the orbit in an ideal lattice, and it grows with machine imperfections and with collisions.

If the particles populate the trajectories in a Gaussian way, the rms beam size at position s is
\sigma_y(s) = \sqrt{\epsilon_y\,\beta_y(s)} .






Note



Worked example. A beam with \epsilon = 1\ \mu\text{m} passing a point where \beta = 25 m has \sigma = \sqrt{(10^{-6})(25)}\ \text{m} = 5 mm. The same beam where \beta = 100 m is twice as wide, 10 mm. Squeezing the beam therefore means making \beta small at the place where it matters. The specific emittance and beam-size calculations of the assignment are left to the assignment.

title: Week 2: Accelerator Physics
text:
Tune and resonances
How many times does a particle oscillate transversely in one trip around the ring?

Definition. The betatron number or tune \nu is the number of betatron oscillations per revolution: \nu = \frac{1}{2\pi}\oint\frac{ds}{\beta(s)} . Equivalently, the total phase advance in one revolution is 2\pi\nu.

Why does the value of \nu matter? Suppose \nu is an integer. Then a particle passes through the same part of the oscillation pattern at the same place on every revolution, about 50 kHz in the lecture’s example. Any imperfection in a single element then kicks the particle in the same direction every turn, and the kicks add up. The lecture calls this a disaster, or more politely a resonance. In general the machine must avoid
p\,\nu_x + q\,\nu_y = \text{integer}
for small integers p and q. The plane of (\nu_x, \nu_y) is crossed by many such lines, and the machine’s operating point must be chosen carefully between them. The Tevatron ran at \nu \approx 19.4. The LHC tune diagram shows injection and collision tunes sitting between the resonance lines, and the 2015 parameter table lists the horizontal and vertical tunes as 64.28/59.31 at injection and 64.31/59.32 at collision. The lecture’s handwritten update refers to the LHC integer parts 59 and 64 and notes that its operating region is even smaller than the Tevatron’s.

Errors in the magnets
Real magnets have finite length, are straight while the reference orbit is curved, and can be displaced from their ideal position. Each of these is a perturbation of the ideal lattice.
A field error \Delta B over a length \Delta s changes the slope of the particle by
\delta x' = \frac{\Delta B}{B}\,\Delta\theta = \frac{\Delta B}{B}\,\frac{\Delta s}{\rho},
using the dipole bend \Delta\theta = \Delta s/\rho from the dipole section. The orbit must still close, otherwise the analysis would be pointless, but it now has a slope discontinuity at the location s_0 of the error. Requiring x(s_0 + C) = x(s_0) with \phi_0 = -\pi\nu_x gives the condition
\delta x' = -2\sqrt{\frac{\epsilon}{\beta(s_0)}}\,\sin(\pi\nu_x) = \frac{\Delta B}{B}\,\frac{\Delta s}{\rho}.
In this closed-orbit calculation \epsilon is the amplitude parameter of the closed orbit itself, not the beam emittance. The condition fixes \sqrt{\epsilon\beta(s_0)}, and the distorted closed orbit becomes
x(s) = A(s)\,\cos\!\left(\int_{s_0}^{s}\frac{ds'}{\beta(s')} - \pi\nu_x\right),
with amplitude
A(s) = \frac{\sqrt{\beta(s_0)\,\beta(s)}}{2\sin\pi\nu_x}\,\frac{\Delta B}{B}\,\frac{\Delta s}{\rho}.
The factor 1/\sin\pi\nu_x diverges when \nu_x is an integer, which is the resonance seen from the orbit’s side. In practice the emittance is the quadrature sum of the injection emittance and growth from imperfections in the focusing structure, the finite momentum spread of the beam, and other effects.

title: Week 2: Accelerator Physics
text:
Luminosity
How often does a collider make the event we want?

Definition. The luminosity \mathcal{L} is the factor that converts a cross section \sigma into an interaction rate: \text{interaction rate} = \mathcal{L}\,\sigma . Its units are events per area per time, for example cm^{-2} s^{-1}.

The luminosity depends on the machine, not on the physics process. It is the accelerator physicist’s figure of merit, and the cross section \sigma is the property of the process. For two counter-rotating bunches with charge densities \rho_1 and \rho_2, the lecture counts the collisions in a small volume d^3x and time dt:
dn = n_b\,f\,\rho_1\,|\vec{v}_1 - \vec{v}_2|\,(\rho_2\,d^3x)\,dt\,\sigma .
Here n_b is the number of bunches and f is the revolution frequency, so f is the rate at which a given bunch meets its partner and n_b f is the total bunch-crossing rate (the lecture writes n for the number of bunches). For a circular collider f = \beta c/2\pi R, which is fixed as \beta\to1.
Integrating over space and over the time it takes the bunches to pass through each other, and taking Gaussian charge distributions with transverse rms sizes \sigma_x, \sigma_y, gives

\mathcal{L} = \frac{n_b f\,N_1 N_2}{2\pi\sqrt{(\sigma_{x1}^2+\sigma_{x2}^2)(\sigma_{y1}^2+\sigma_{y2}^2)}} .

Here N_1 and N_2 are the particle numbers per bunch. If all four transverse sizes are equal, as in the Tevatron, the denominator becomes 4\pi\sigma^2:
\mathcal{L} = \frac{n_b f\,N_1 N_2}{4\pi\sigma^2}.
To first order the bunch length does not appear, because every particle of one bunch eventually meets every particle of the other. That fails if the betatron wavelength is comparable to the bunch length.

Luminosity in terms of emittance
Can we tie this back to the machine optics? Yes, using the beam size \sigma = \sqrt{\epsilon\beta} from the envelope section. The optics are designed so that \beta(s_0) = \beta^{*} is a minimum at the collision point, so the beam size there is \sigma = \sqrt{\epsilon\beta^{*}} and

\mathcal{L} = \frac{n_b f\,N_1 N_2}{4\pi\sqrt{\epsilon_x\epsilon_y\,\beta^{*}_{x}\beta^{*}_{y}}} .

Small \beta^* and small emittance mean a small, dense collision region and a high luminosity. There is a limit, though. Near the collision point the envelope grows as \beta(s) \approx \beta^{*} + s^2/\beta^{*}, so squeezing \beta^* too far makes the beam blow up quickly on either side of the collision point. If this happens over a distance shorter than the bunch length, the ends of the bunches no longer meet at the waist, and \mathcal{L} stops improving.

Figure 3. The envelope \beta(s) is smallest at the collision point. If it grows too fast away from that point, the ends of a long bunch are collided at a larger beam size.





Design choices behind \mathcal{L}
The lecture reads the luminosity formula as a list of wishes, each limited by a physical effect.

Many bunches (n_b large). The Tevatron in its first run used 6 bunches, spaced by 3.5 \mus. The lecture quotes about 150 bunch slots at 132 ns for the second run; the Tevatron in fact ran 36 bunches per beam at a spacing of 396 ns, and the 132 ns plan was not carried out. The lecture’s LHC update gives about 2500 bunches and a 25 ns spacing (the 2015 parameter table lists up to 2748 in the nominal scheme).
Many particles per bunch (N_1, N_2 large). Too high a charge density causes repulsion and beam blow-up, and the source of the particles limits the total (antiproton sources and cooling rates in the Tevatron). The LHC uses protons for both beams, at roughly 1.1 to 1.3\times10^{11} per bunch (the nominal value is 1.15\times10^{11}, and the lecture’s handwritten update quotes 1.5\times10^{11}).
Small beam area. Requires small \beta^*, but \beta(s) is then large nearby, which limits the acceptance of the machine. The emittance grows with machine imperfections and with the collisions themselves.

The lecture quotes a Tevatron luminosity of a few \times10^{31}\ \text{cm}^{-2}\text{s}^{-1} at peak performance, which matches Run I (near 2\times10^{31}); Run II later reached about 4\times10^{32}\ \text{cm}^{-2}\text{s}^{-1}. The LHC’s nominal design luminosity is 10^{34}\ \text{cm}^{-2}\text{s}^{-1}, and the lecture’s update quotes a value above that, which Run 2 operation reached. A fixed target of solid matter can reach about 10^{37}\ \text{cm}^{-2}\text{s}^{-1}, because a bunch cannot be packed as densely as a solid. The lecture notes that the LHC can still compete with a fixed target on luminosity, and that the real disadvantage of a fixed target is the energy available, taken up in the section on colliders.


The beam-beam force and the tune shift
A bunch of charged particles is a charge distribution, and the electric and magnetic fields it produces act on other particles. Two bunches, moving with velocities \vec{v}_1 and \vec{v}_2, exert on each other the transverse force
F^{\perp}_{12} = e_1\,\gamma_2\,(1 - \beta_1\beta_2)\,E'^{\perp}_2 .
Here E'^{\perp}_2 is the transverse field in the rest frame of bunch 2, and the factor \gamma_2(1-\beta_1\beta_2) comes from transforming the electric and magnetic fields to the laboratory frame. Two conclusions follow:

For beams moving in the same direction with \beta\to1 the force tends to zero. Relativistic beams are stable against transverse space-charge forces (slower ones are not).
For colliding beams, \beta_1\to-\beta_1 and the factor becomes (1+\beta_1\beta_2). The beams see a strong defocusing force as they pass through the oncoming bunch.

This force changes the tune. The lecture defines the tune shift as the phase accumulated per orbit from an extra focusing strength K(s),
\Delta\nu_x \equiv \frac{1}{4\pi}\oint ds\,\beta_x(s)\,K(s),
which is like the quadrupole strength but here arising from imperfections and from the other bunches. For the antiproton and proton bunches,
\Delta\nu^{\bar p}_x = \frac{r_{\bar p}\,\beta_{x\bar p}\,N_p}{2\pi\gamma_{\bar p}\,\sigma_{xp}(\sigma_{xp}+\sigma_{yp})}, \qquad
\Delta\nu^{p}_x = \frac{r_{p}\,\beta_{xp}\,N_{\bar p}}{2\pi\gamma_{p}\,\sigma_{x\bar p}(\sigma_{x\bar p}+\sigma_{y\bar p})},
where r is the classical particle radius. The luminosity is proportional to the product of the two tune shifts, \mathcal{L}\sim\Delta\nu^{\bar p}\Delta\nu^{p}. Empirically, the tune shifts are limited to about 0.005 for hadron beams (the Tevatron) and about 0.05 for electron beams (LEP). Beyond those values the tune gets too close to integer resonances, beam instabilities set in, and the beam is lost.
Since \Delta\nu^{\bar p}\propto N_p, raising the intensity of one beam alone does not help. The gain is in matching N_p and N_{\bar p} (or the two tune shifts) and pushing both toward the physical limit in a balanced way.

title: Week 2: Accelerator Physics
text:
Why colliders?
If a fixed target can reach a higher luminosity, why build colliders? The answer is the energy available for making new particles, which is the centre-of-mass energy E_{\text{cm}} = \sqrt{s}, with
s = (p_1 + p_2)_\mu (p_1 + p_2)^\mu = m_1^2 + m_2^2 + 2\big(E_1E_2 - \vec{p}_1\cdot\vec{p}_2\big).
For a projectile of energy E on a fixed target of mass M at rest, when E \gg M, m,
\sqrt{s_{\text{FT}}} \approx \sqrt{2ME} .
For two beams of equal energy E in a collider, \vec{p}_1 = -\vec{p}_2 and E_1 = E_2, so
\sqrt{s_{\text{collider}}} \approx 2E .






Note



Worked example. For E = 1 TeV and a proton target, M \approx 0.94 GeV, the fixed-target energy is \sqrt{2 \times 0.94 \times 1000}\ \text{GeV}\approx 43 GeV. For a collider with two 1 TeV beams it is 2000 GeV. The fixed target wastes most of the beam energy on the motion of the products, while the collider sees the entire beam energy in its centre-of-mass frame.


A collider trades a luminosity disadvantage for a large gain in the energy available.

title: Week 2: Accelerator Physics
text:
The basics of acceleration
How is energy added to the beam? The earliest accelerators used a static electric field between two electrodes, so a particle crossing a potential difference \Delta V gains energy e\Delta V. Two limits stop this from scaling:

Breakdown. In dry air breakdown occurs at about 3 MV/m, when electrons ionised by the field gain enough energy between collisions to ionise further.
Surface defects. A defect on a surface, such as a Van de Graaff terminal or a cavity wall, concentrates the field to much higher values around the imperfection.

The fix is to use alternating fields, the radio-frequency or RF structure. The field is not present “long enough” for breakdown to occur. A linear machine can chain many such gaps with alternating potentials, giving energy E = neV after n stages. In practice the alternating potentials come from a longitudinal electric field in a resonant cavity through which the beam passes.

Orbit length and RF frequency
For simplicity take one RF cavity in the ring. The RF must be tuned so that a reference particle arrives at the cavity in time with the field on every turn. The RF angular frequency is a whole number h times the orbital frequency \omega_0:
\omega_{\text{rf}} = h\,\omega_0, \qquad \omega_0 = \frac{2\pi}{\tau_{\text{orbit}}}, \qquad \tau_{\text{orbit}} = \frac{L_{\text{part}}}{v_{\text{part}}} .

Definition. The integer h is the harmonic number of the machine. It is the number of places around the ring where a particle can arrive in time with the RF field. The frequency \omega_0 is the revolution (orbital) angular frequency, and the RF frequency \omega_{\text{rf}} = h\omega_0 must be changed to follow it as the particles are accelerated.

For the CERN SPS h = 4620 (and 1113 for the Fermilab Main Ring), so the SPS could in principle hold 4620 bunches. As a proton-antiproton collider it ran with three bunches per beam, later six.
Two effects could put a particle out of time with the RF:

A particle off axis takes a different path length, L \neq L_{\text{ideal}}.
A particle off momentum has a different speed, v \neq v_{\text{ideal}}.

Together they change the arrival time by
\frac{\Delta T}{T} = \frac{\Delta L}{L} - \frac{\Delta v}{v} .
A faster particle arrives sooner, and a longer path arrives later. Both terms can be written in terms of the momentum error. From p = \gamma m v,
\frac{\Delta v}{v} = \frac{1}{\gamma^2}\,\frac{\Delta p}{p}.
The path length of an off-momentum particle also changes, and the lecture defines a machine parameter \gamma_T through
\frac{\Delta L}{L} = \frac{1}{\gamma_T^2}\,\frac{\Delta p}{p}.
Combining the two gives

\frac{\Delta T}{T} = \left(\frac{1}{\gamma_T^{2}} - \frac{1}{\gamma^{2}}\right)\frac{\Delta p}{p}.

The bracket changes sign at \gamma = \gamma_T. The spread in \Delta p across the beam is called the longitudinal emittance, by analogy with the transverse case.


Phase stability and transition
What does it mean to arrive “in time” with the RF? The voltage across the cavity is V = V_0\sin(\omega_{\text{rf}}t). The reference particle arrives at the synchronous phase \phi_s and gains energy E_s = eV_0\sin\phi_s per turn. A particle at a different phase \phi gains
\Delta E = eV_0\,(\sin\phi - \sin\phi_s).
The two regimes below and above \gamma_T behave differently.

Below transition (\gamma < \gamma_T, so \Delta T/T has the sign of -\Delta p/p), a more energetic particle is faster and arrives sooner. The stable synchronous phase is on the rising side of the RF wave, and a particle that arrives late gets more energy on the next turn while an early one gets less. The stable region in (\phi, \Delta E) space is an ellipse-like island bounded by a curve called the separatrix, and the whole island is an RF bucket.
Above transition (\gamma > \gamma_T), extra energy means a longer orbit time, so the stable point sits on the other side of the sinusoid.

The lecture then does this quantitatively. For a reference particle on the central orbit of radius R_0, the revolution time is t_{\text{rev}} = 2\pi R_0/\beta c and \omega_{\text{RF}} = h\beta c/R_0. An energy change \Delta E changes the speed and momentum by
\frac{\Delta\beta}{\beta} = \frac{1}{\gamma^2\beta^2}\,\frac{\Delta E}{E}, \qquad \frac{\Delta p}{p} = \frac{1}{\beta^2}\,\frac{\Delta E}{E},
and the radius by \Delta R = \bar\eta\,\Delta p/p. The change in revolution time is
\Delta t_r = \frac{2\pi R_0}{\beta^3 c}\left(\frac{\bar\eta}{R_0} - \frac{1}{\gamma^2}\right)\frac{\Delta E}{E}, \qquad \gamma_T^2 \equiv \frac{R_0}{\bar\eta}.
Below transition \Delta t_r < 0, and above transition \Delta t_r > 0. The RF phase shift a particle accumulates in one turn is
\Delta\phi = \omega_{\text{RF}}\,\Delta t_r = \bar\Phi\,\frac{\Delta E}{E},
with
\bar\Phi = \frac{2\pi h}{\beta^2}\left(\frac{1}{\gamma_T^{2}} - \frac{1}{\gamma^{2}}\right).
The per-turn energy kick is \Delta E = eV_0(\sin\phi - \sin\phi_s). Real accelerators give only a small kick per turn, so after many turns the changes accumulate and we can treat the turn number n (a count of turns here, not of bunches) as continuous:
\frac{d\phi}{dn} = \bar\Phi\,\frac{\Delta E}{E}, \qquad \frac{d}{dn}\!\left(\frac{\Delta E}{E}\right) = \frac{eV_0}{E}\,(\sin\phi - \sin\phi_s).
Combining them,
\frac{d^2\phi}{dn^2} = \frac{eV_0}{E}\,\bar\Phi\,(\sin\phi - \sin\phi_s).
For a small departure \phi = \phi_s + \Delta\phi we have \sin\phi - \sin\phi_s \approx \Delta\phi\cos\phi_s, and the equation becomes
\frac{d^2(\Delta\phi)}{dn^2} - \frac{eV_0}{E}\,\bar\Phi\cos\phi_s\;\Delta\phi = 0 .

\bar\Phi\,\cos\phi_s < 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{stable oscillations}.

The sign of \bar\Phi flips at transition (below transition \bar\Phi<0, above it \bar\Phi>0), so to keep the beam stable the RF phase must jump from \phi_s to \pi - \phi_s as transition is crossed. That operation loses particles. It is therefore preferable to build a series of machines of increasing energy and different radii, so that the beam is injected already above transition. This is one of several reasons for an accelerator complex of boosters. Others are the limit of a single machine (each bunch of the final machine is filled with the full complement of the previous one) and the use of smaller machines for other purposes, such as making antiprotons or fixed-target physics.
The lecture leaves as an exercise for the students the derivation of \gamma_T, a property of the machine that depends mainly on the machine radius and the size of the betatron oscillations.


Synchrotron oscillations

Definition. Synchrotron oscillations are the oscillations in energy (and phase) of a particle from ahead of to behind the reference particle. The number of turns per oscillation is n_{\text{sync}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{E}{eV_0\,|\bar\Phi\cos\phi_s|}}\ \text{turns.}

In a proton machine this is several hundred turns, and the synchrotron frequency ranges from 0 (exactly at transition, where \bar\Phi\to0) up to about 1000 Hz. That is slow for anything travelling near the speed of light.


Phase space of stable oscillations
Multiplying the equation of motion by d\phi/dn and integrating over n gives an energy-like conservation law:
\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{d\phi}{dn}\right)^2 + \frac{eV_0\bar\Phi}{E}\left(\cos\phi + \phi\sin\phi_s\right) = \text{constant}.
The first term plays the role of kinetic energy and the second of potential energy, so the motion is that of a particle in a potential that looks like a tilted row of wells. A particle with a total “energy” below the top of a well is trapped and oscillates (stable). One above it runs off to the next well and is lost from the bucket (unstable). The solutions can be found numerically. For the \bar\eta>0 case in the lecture’s figure, the bucket is largest for \phi_s = \pi and shrinks as \phi_s moves through 5\pi/6 to 2\pi/3: accelerating harder, that is a larger energy gain per turn, leaves less room for stable motion. How large \Delta E and \Delta\phi can be while the beam stays longitudinally stable is a problem in the assignment.

title: Week 2: Accelerator Physics
text:
Summary






Note



Key takeaways from Week 2:

Three fields, three jobs. Dipoles bend (\rho = p/0.3B), quadrupoles focus (F\propto p), and RF cavities accelerate.
Strong focusing. Alternating focusing and defocusing quadrupoles (FODO) give net focusing, and the motion is described by transfer matrices that multiply along the ring.
Betatron motion. Each plane obeys Hill’s equation. Its solution y=\sqrt{\epsilon\beta(s)}\cos(\phi+\delta) splits into a machine part, \beta(s) (the envelope), and a beam part, the emittance \epsilon.
Tune and resonances. The tune \nu=\tfrac{1}{2\pi}\oint ds/\beta must avoid integer and low-order resonances, otherwise field errors blow the orbit up like 1/\sin\pi\nu.
Luminosity. \mathcal{L}=n_bfN_1N_2/(4\pi\sqrt{\epsilon_x\epsilon_y\beta^*_x\beta^*_y}) is set by bunch count, bunch charge, and a small beam at the collision point. It is limited by the beam-beam tune shift (\lesssim0.005 for hadrons) and by squeezing \beta^* too far.
Colliders win on energy. \sqrt{s}\approx2E for a collider against \sqrt{2ME} for a fixed target.
RF acceleration. Phase stability needs \bar\Phi\cos\phi_s<0. The sign of \bar\Phi flips at transition energy, and the resulting particle losses are one reason for an accelerator complex.

title: Week 3: Future Colliders
text:
Why a bigger ring is not enough
Overview. Week 2 built a circular collider from dipoles, quadrupoles and RF cavities, and showed that a collider wins over a fixed target because the centre-of-mass energy is \sqrt{s}\approx 2E. This week asks what stops us from simply building the next ring at a higher energy. The answer for electrons is synchrotron radiation: a charged particle bent onto a circle radiates, and the loss grows so fast with energy that it sets the size of the machine. The lecture uses this one effect to sort the proposals for the next generation of colliders: linear electron colliders that never bend the beam, hadron colliders that bend heavier particles, and a muon collider that tries to keep the advantages of both.
The running examples are the proposals the slides compare: the ILC and CLIC linear colliders, the FCC-hh and HE-LHC hadron colliders measured against the LHC, and a muon collider. Two Week 2 results are restated where we need them: the bending radius \rho = p/0.3B (momentum in GeV/c, field in tesla, radius in metres), and the interaction rate \mathcal{L}\,\sigma.
The related problem set is the Accelerator Problems sheet, item 4 (a 50 TeV on 50 TeV proton collider). These notes explain the concepts that item depends on. The specific calculations it asks for are left to the assignment.
Week 2 gave a direct recipe for a higher-energy ring. At fixed dipole field B, the bending radius grows in proportion to the momentum,
\rho = \frac{p}{0.3\,B},
so doubling the beam energy at the same field doubles the radius of the arcs. Stronger magnets shrink the ring, and a bigger tunnel raises the energy. If that were the whole story, the energy of a collider would be limited only by money and magnet technology.
For protons it nearly is, and the hadron proposals below are built along exactly these lines. For electrons a second limit arrives first. The particle loses energy every time it is bent, and that loss grows with the fourth power of the beam energy.

title: Week 3: Future Colliders
text:
Synchrotron radiation
Why does bending a beam cost energy?
A direct consequence of Maxwell’s equations is that an accelerated charge radiates. A particle moving on a circle is accelerating even at constant speed, because its direction changes, and the acceleration points toward the centre of the circle, perpendicular to the motion.

Definition. Synchrotron radiation is the electromagnetic radiation emitted by a charged particle moving at relativistic speed with an acceleration perpendicular to its velocity, as in the magnetic field of a dipole.

For a particle of charge q on an arc of radius \rho, the radiated power is given by the relativistic form of the Larmor formula, which the slides quote in SI units (the source cited is Jackson, Classical Electrodynamics, Chapter 14):

P_\gamma = \frac{q^2}{6\pi\varepsilon_0 c^3}\,a^2\gamma^4 = \frac{q^2 c}{6\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{\beta^4\gamma^4}{\rho^2}.

Here \varepsilon_0 is the vacuum permittivity, a is the magnitude of the acceleration, \beta = v/c, and \gamma is the Lorentz factor, \gamma = E/mc^2. The two forms agree because the acceleration on a circle is a = v^2/\rho = \beta^2c^2/\rho.
The factor \gamma^4 carries the physics. At a fixed beam energy E, a lighter particle has a larger \gamma, and the power climbs as the fourth power of \gamma. A tighter bend (smaller \rho) also raises the power.

Figure 1. The velocity is tangent to the orbit and the acceleration points to the centre. A relativistic particle emits its radiation into a narrow cone of opening angle about 1/\gamma around its direction of motion, and it does so all along the bent part of its path.




Energy lost per turn
Power is energy per unit time. What matters to the RF system of Week 2 is the energy a particle loses on each trip around the ring, because the cavities must put that much back every turn. If the bends all have radius \rho, the particle spends a time 2\pi\rho/\beta c in the dipoles per turn, so the loss per turn is

U_0 = P_\gamma\,\frac{2\pi\rho}{\beta c} = \frac{q^2\,\beta^3\gamma^4}{3\,\varepsilon_0\,\rho}.

Only the bends count here. Straight sections, where the particle is not accelerated, add circumference but not loss, which is one reason real rings are larger than 2\pi\rho.






Note



Worked example. Take an electron ring with beam energy E = 100 GeV and bending radius \rho = 3000 m. Then \gamma = 100\ \text{GeV}/0.511\ \text{MeV} \approx 1.96\times10^{5} and \gamma^4 \approx 1.47\times10^{21}. With q = e and \beta \approx 1, U_0 \approx \frac{(1.60\times10^{-19})^2\,(1.47\times10^{21})}{3\,(8.85\times10^{-12})\,(3000)}\ \text{J} \approx 4.7\times10^{-10}\ \text{J}, with the charge in coulombs, \varepsilon_0 in F/m and \rho in metres. That is about 3 GeV, so each electron loses roughly 3% of its energy on every turn, and the RF system must restore it every turn. Doubling the beam energy at the same radius multiplies the loss by 2^4 = 16.


This steep growth is why the proposals below either stop bending electrons or bend something heavier.

title: Week 3: Future Colliders
text:
Electrons, protons and muons
Which particle should we collide? The slides compare three choices, and each trades one advantage against another.
Electrons are point-like. When an electron meets a positron, the whole beam energy goes into the collision, so \sqrt{s} = 2E is the energy actually available for making new particles. Their limit is the energy we can reach. A circular electron collider is limited by synchrotron radiation. A linear collider avoids bending, but can collide each accelerated bunch only once.
Protons are not point-like. A proton is made of quarks and gluons, collectively called partons, and a collision is really a collision between one parton from each proton. Each parton carries only a fraction of the proton’s energy, so the energy of the hard collision is a fraction of \sqrt{s}, and it varies from event to event. In exchange, the synchrotron loss is much lower. It is still not negligible at the LHC, where the radiated power ends up in the superconducting magnets.
Muons might give the best of both. A muon is point-like like the electron, but about 200 times heavier, so it radiates far less. Its problem is that it decays, with a lifetime at rest of about 2 \mus.
How much less does a heavier particle radiate? At a fixed beam energy E and radius \rho, with \beta \approx 1, the loss per turn depends on the mass only through \gamma = E/mc^2:
U_0 \propto \frac{\gamma^4}{\rho} = \frac{1}{\rho}\left(\frac{E}{mc^2}\right)^{4} \propto \frac{1}{m^4}.
The fourth power of the mass ratio sets the suppression.

title: Week 3: Future Colliders
text:
Linear colliders
If bending an electron beam is what costs energy, why not accelerate it in a straight line?

Definition. A linear collider accelerates two beams in long straight accelerators (linacs) aimed at each other, and collides them once at a single interaction point. The beams are then dumped.

A linear collider has no synchrotron radiation limit, because the beam is never bent in the main linacs. The cost is that each accelerated bunch is used once. In a ring of Week 2 the same bunch returns and collides at the revolution frequency f, so the luminosity carries the factor n_b f (bunches times revolutions per second). A linear collider replaces that with the rate at which new bunches are accelerated, which is far lower. To still reach a useful luminosity, the beams must be squeezed to extremely small sizes at the collision point.
The two proposals in the slides are the International Linear Collider (ILC), with superconducting cavities, and the Compact Linear Collider (CLIC), with normal-conducting copper structures driven by a second, high-current drive beam. Three rows explain the design. The accelerating gradient is the energy gained per metre of accelerating structure, so it sets how long the linacs must be. The beam sizes at the interaction point are a few hundred nanometres wide and a few nanometres tall, much smaller than in a ring; this is how a linear collider recovers luminosity at a repetition rate of a few tens of hertz. The site length follows from the gradient and the beam energy. Other slides in the deck quote slightly different bunch spacings for the ILC (360 ns and 333 ns), because they come from different versions of the design.






Note



Worked example. How long must the accelerating structure of one linac be? Each beam must reach half the centre-of-mass energy. For CLIC at 3 TeV, one beam needs 1.5 TeV = 1.5\times10^{6} MeV, and at 100 MV/m an electron gains 100 MeV per metre, so the structure needs at least \frac{1.5\times10^{6}\ \text{MeV}}{100\ \text{MeV/m}} = 1.5\times10^{4}\ \text{m} = 15\ \text{km}. The CLIC layout on the slides shows each main linac as 21 km long. The difference is room for focusing magnets, instrumentation and the gaps between structures. At the ILC gradient of about 32 MV/m, the same 1.5 TeV beam would need about 47 km of structure for one linac alone, which is one reason the ILC is proposed at a lower energy.



The energy spread of the collisions
Is every collision at the nominal energy? Not quite. Because the bunches are so dense at the collision point, each particle feels the strong field of the oncoming bunch and radiates as it passes through it. This radiation is called beamstrahlung. A particle that has radiated collides at slightly less than the full beam energy.
The slides show the resulting spectrum of collision energies for CLIC at 0.5, 1, 3 and 5 TeV. Each has a sharp peak at the nominal energy, E/E_0 = 1, and a tail toward lower energies. The tail is larger at higher energies. This is what the second luminosity row of the table measures: at 3 TeV only about a third of the total luminosity (2.0 out of 5.9) is within 1% of the peak energy.

title: Week 3: Future Colliders
text:
Muon colliders
Can we have point-like collisions without the radiation of electrons? A muon collider is the slides’ answer.

Muons, like electrons, are point-like projectiles. All of the beam energy is available in the collision for making new particles.
Their bending radiation is smaller than that of electrons by the factor \approx(m_\mu/m_e)^4 \approx 200^4, the 10^{9} of the previous section. A muon beam can therefore be bent around a ring, and reused turn after turn.

The obstacle is the lifetime. A muon at rest decays in about 2.2 \mus (the slides round this to 2 \mus). A muon moving at nearly c lives longer in the laboratory because of time dilation: its laboratory lifetime is \gamma\tau.






Note



Worked example. Take a muon of energy 1.5 TeV. With m_\mu c^2 = 105.7 MeV, \gamma = 1.5\times10^{6}/105.7 \approx 1.4\times10^{4}. Its laboratory lifetime is \gamma\tau \approx (1.4\times10^{4})(2.2\ \mu\text{s}) \approx 31\ \text{ms}, in which it travels c\gamma\tau \approx 9000 km. In a ring 10 km around, that is about 900 turns on average before it decays. That is long enough to make collisions, but the whole chain of producing, preparing and accelerating the muons has to happen quickly.


The slides show the stages of a muon collider in order:

A proton driver (a superconducting linac, an accumulator and a buncher) makes intense proton pulses.
In the front end, the protons hit a target. The pions produced decay into muons, which are captured in a solenoid.
The muons come out with a large spread in position and momentum. Cooling reduces this spread, which is the emittance of Week 2, before the beam is accelerated.
Acceleration uses linacs and fast-acting rings (recirculating linacs, fixed-field alternating gradient rings, or rapid cycling synchrotrons).
The collider ring brings \mu^+ and \mu^- into collision, at energies from a Higgs factory up to about 10 TeV.

The slides also show an alternative source, LEMMA, which would make muon pairs from positrons hitting electrons in a target. The muons come out with a small emittance, so less charge is needed in the collider rings, which gives lower backgrounds in the detector.
Decays also cause a detector problem. Muons that decay near the interaction region produce electrons, and these shower in the machine components and send a spray of particles into the detector. The slides call this the muon beam halo background, and show a simulation of tracks entering the detector from the beam line.

Protons radiate far less than electrons, but the factor \gamma^4 catches up at these energies. The radiated power per beam rises from 3.6 kW at the LHC to 2400 kW at FCC-hh. Why does this matter for a superconducting machine? The magnet cold mass of the LHC runs at 1.9 K, and heat removed at that temperature is expensive. The radiation is therefore intercepted by a beam screen, a liner inside the beam pipe held at 40–60 K, where cooling is much cheaper. The slides show the LHC dipole cross-section with its beam screens and thermal shields, and the screen design proposed for FCC-hh and HE-LHC.


Pileup
How many proton collisions happen each time two bunches cross? Week 2 gave the interaction rate as \mathcal{L}\,\sigma. Dividing by the rate at which bunches cross gives the mean number of collisions per crossing.

Definition. Pileup is the set of extra proton-proton collisions that occur in the same bunch crossing as the collision of interest. Its mean number per crossing is \mu = \frac{\mathcal{L}\,\sigma_{\text{inel}}}{f_{\text{BC}}}, where \sigma_{\text{inel}} is the inelastic proton-proton cross section and f_{\text{BC}} is the bunch-crossing rate, the n_b f of Week 2.

Every extra collision adds tracks and energy to the detector that have nothing to do with the event being studied.






Note



Worked example. The slides’ table of detector challenges gives, for the LHC, \mathcal{L} = 10^{34} cm^{-2}s^{-1}, \sigma_{\text{inel}} = 80 mb and f_{\text{BC}} = 31.6 MHz. With 1\ \text{mb} = 10^{-27} cm^2, \mu = \frac{(10^{34})(80\times10^{-27})}{31.6\times10^{6}} \approx 25. For FCC-hh the same table gives \mathcal{L} = 30\times10^{34} cm^{-2}s^{-1}, \sigma_{\text{inel}} = 103 mb and f_{\text{BC}} = 32.5 MHz, which gives \mu \approx 950. Both match the pileup row of that table. Another slide quotes about 1000 for the same FCC-hh configuration, the same value rounded.


The bunch-crossing rate is lower than the 40 MHz that a 25 ns spacing suggests because not every bunch slot around the ring is filled.
The same table lists the other detector challenges that grow with energy and luminosity. The rate of charged tracks rises from about 59 GHz at the LHC to about 3900 GHz at FCC-hh. The total ionising dose expected at 2.5 cm from the beam rises from about 1.3 MGy to about 270 MGy. A detector at FCC-hh would have to separate about a thousand collisions per crossing and survive two hundred times the radiation dose of an LHC detector.

text:
Electron-proton colliders
The last option in the slides collides an electron beam with a proton beam. The proposals add a 60 GeV electron accelerator to an existing or future proton ring: the LHeC with the LHC’s 7 TeV protons, and FCC-he with 50 TeV protons.
For two head-on beams of energies E_1 and E_2 much larger than the masses, the centre-of-mass energy from Week 2 reduces to s \approx 4E_1E_2.






Note



Worked example. For LHeC, \sqrt{s} \approx 2\sqrt{(60\ \text{GeV})(7000\ \text{GeV})} \approx 1.3 TeV. For FCC-he, \sqrt{s} \approx 2\sqrt{(60)(50\,000)}\ \text{GeV} \approx 3.5 TeV. Both match the slides’ table.

title: Week 3: Future Colliders
text:
Summary






Note



Key takeaways from Week 3:

Bending costs energy. A relativistic charge on an arc radiates P_\gamma \propto \gamma^4/\rho^2 and loses U_0 \propto \gamma^4/\rho per turn, which the RF must replace every turn.
Mass decides the loss. At fixed energy and radius the loss scales as 1/m^4: muons radiate about 10^{9} times less than electrons, and protons about 10^{13} times less.
Three ways forward. Linear electron colliders (ILC, CLIC) avoid bending but use each bunch once, so they need nanometre beams. Hadron colliders (HE-LHC, FCC-hh) bend protons but deliver only a fraction of \sqrt{s} to each parton collision. Muon colliders are point-like and can be bent, but the muons decay.
Linac length. The accelerating gradient sets the length of a linear collider: CLIC at 100 MV/m needs at least 15 km of structure for each 1.5 TeV beam.
Hadron rings still radiate. At FCC-hh the synchrotron power reaches megawatts per beam, intercepted by beam screens above the magnet temperature.
Pileup grows with luminosity. \mu = \mathcal{L}\sigma_{\text{inel}}/f_{\text{BC}} is about 25 at the LHC and about 950 at FCC-hh.



Next week: Week 4 turns from colliders to rare event searches at low energy: how their backgrounds are suppressed, and how their detectors are cooled to millikelvin temperatures.

title: Week 4: Rare Event Searches and Cryogenics
text:
Rare event searches
Overview. Weeks 2 and 3 built colliders, where the problem is making enough collisions at high enough energy. This week turns to the other half of the course, the experiments of the Week 1 energy ladder that look for something extremely rare at low energy: a dark matter particle bumping a nucleus, a nucleus decaying in a way never yet seen, a neutrino scattering coherently from a whole nucleus. For these experiments the difficulty is not making events but recognising the few that matter among everything else the detector sees. In Week 1 we called the things we look for signal and the look-alikes background. This week makes that distinction quantitative.
The chapter follows the two lecture decks in order. The first, Laboratories for rare event search experiments, designs an ideal dark matter detector: how many signal events to expect, where the background comes from, and the five steps used to suppress it. The second, Battle with noise: cooling it down, explains why many of these detectors run at temperatures of a few thousandths of a kelvin, which material properties matter on the way down, and the machines (pulse tubes, dilution refrigerators, magnetic refrigerators) that get them there. The running example throughout is the slides’ own: the SuperCDMS dark matter experiment at SNOLAB and the cryostats that cool it.
The related problem set is eHEP Homework 2, items 1 to 3 (the heat load of a cryostat cable, a stainless steel line into the mixing chamber, and the cavern gamma background in DRU). Items 4 and 5 of HW4 and item 5 of the Third Problem Set also lean on ideas introduced here. These notes explain the concepts those items depend on. The specific calculations are left to the assignments.
What do the experiments of the low-energy half of the course have in common?
They all search for a process so rare that, in a detector of tens or hundreds of kilograms, only a handful of events are expected per year. The lecture calls this finding a needle in a haystack, and gives three examples, with numbers benchmarked for xenon-based experiments:
Two features recur. The expected number of signal events is quoted per unit of mass times time, because doubling the detector mass or the running time doubles the number of chances for the rare process to happen. And the signal sits in a narrow band of energy, which is where all of the effort to remove background is concentrated.

title: Week 4: Rare Event Searches and Cryogenics
text:
Background and the DRU
How do we compare the background in two different experiments, with different masses, running times and energy windows?

Definition. The exposure of an experiment is its target mass times its live time, for example in kg·day. The region of interest (ROI) is the window of deposited energy in which the signal is expected.

For a process with a small cross section, the number of events grows in proportion to the exposure, and over a narrow ROI the spectrum is often roughly flat. It is therefore natural to quote a background rate per unit exposure and per unit energy.

Definition. The differential rate unit (DRU) is one event per keV of deposited energy, per kg of detector, per day: 1\ \text{DRU} = 1\ \text{event}/(\text{keV}\cdot\text{kg}\cdot\text{day}).

The lecturer’s benchmark numbers for the background level of an environment:

Unshielded laboratory: about 10,000 DRU. This is dominated by gamma rays from the radioactive isotopes potassium-40, thorium-232 and uranium-238 in the walls. At sea level, cosmic-ray muons also arrive at about 1 per minute per cm².
Useful environment: about 100 DRU.
Good environment: below 10 DRU, and ideally far below.







Note



Worked example. How many background events does a “useful” 100 DRU environment give in one kilogram running for one year, in a 10 keV-wide ROI? Multiply the rate by each factor of the exposure and the window: N = (100\ \text{keV}^{-1}\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,\text{day}^{-1})(10\ \text{keV})(1\ \text{kg})(365\ \text{days}) \approx 3.7\times10^{5}. A “good” 10 DRU environment gives about 3.7\times10^{4}, and an unshielded lab about 3.7\times10^{7}. A WIMP search expects fewer than one signal event in thirty such kilogram-years. Even a good environment leaves the signal outnumbered by about a million to one, which is why the rest of the first deck is about removing background and telling the remainder apart from signal.


The slides show the same comparison for a CEvNS search. The predicted Standard Model rate is a few hundred DRU at recoil energies of 1 eV, falls steeply above about 0.1 keV, and vanishes near 1.3 keV. The plot marks an assumed electron-recoil background at 100 DRU and a nuclear-recoil background near 5 DRU: the signal rises above the electron-recoil level only below about 0.1 keV. Dotted curves show how possible new physics (a neutrino magnetic moment, a sterile neutrino, a light Z' boson) would change the spectrum, which is what such an experiment hopes to measure. A low energy threshold is what makes the signal visible at all.

Noise and background
The words “noise” and “background” are sometimes used interchangeably, both meaning “whatever is not signal”. The lecture separates them when it matters:

Noise is present continuously. It comes from physics (thermal motion of electrons, for instance), but usually not from particle interactions. It is the subject of the second half of this chapter and of a later lecture on noise modelling.
Background comes mostly from particle interactions, known or unknown. Each background event produces a pulse in the detector, just as a signal event does.
crumbs: 5  Week 4: Rare Event Searches and Cryogenics

title: Week 4: Rare Event Searches and Cryogenics
text:
The dark matter wind
Where would a WIMP signal come from?
Our galaxy is thought to sit inside a roughly spherical halo of dark matter. The Sun moves through this halo at about 220 km/s, so in the frame of the Earth the dark matter arrives as a wind, which happens to blow from the direction of the constellation Cygnus. The slides quote a flux of about 10^{5} particles per cm² per second, or about 20 million passing through a hand every second.

Where the rate comes from
The flux follows from a density and a speed. If the local dark matter mass density is \rho_0 and each particle has mass m_\chi, the number density is n = \rho_0/m_\chi, and the flux is n v.






Note



Worked example. A commonly used value of the local density is \rho_0 \approx 0.3 GeV/cm³ (this number is not on the slides). For a WIMP of mass m_\chi = 100 GeV/c^2, n = 0.3/100 = 3\times10^{-3} cm^{-3}. With v = 220 km/s = 2.2\times10^{7} cm/s, n v \approx (3\times10^{-3}\ \text{cm}^{-3})(2.2\times10^{7}\ \text{cm/s}) \approx 7\times10^{4}\ \text{cm}^{-2}\,\text{s}^{-1}, which is the slides’ \sim10^{5}. The “20 million per hand” corresponds to a hand of about 2\times10^{7}/10^{5} = 200 cm².


Each nucleus in the detector then interacts at a rate n v \sigma, where \sigma is the WIMP-nucleus cross section. With twenty million particles crossing a hand each second and only about one interaction per kilogram per year, \sigma must be extraordinarily small.
crumbs: 5  Week 4: Rare Event Searches and Cryogenics

title: Week 4: Rare Event Searches and Cryogenics
text:
The signal rate
How does the expected signal spectrum depend on the WIMP, the target and the galaxy?
The lecture (adapted from a TASI 2016 lecture) writes the differential rate of nuclear recoils, in events/(keV·kg·day), as a product of three factors:

\frac{dR}{dE_R} = \frac{\sigma_0}{m_\chi}\;\frac{F^2(E_R)}{m_r^2}\;\frac{\rho_0\,T(E_R)}{v_0\sqrt{\pi}}

The slides colour the three fractions, from left to right, as particle theory, nuclear structure and astrophysics. Here E_R is the kinetic energy given to the recoiling nucleus, \sigma_0 is the WIMP-nucleus cross section at zero momentum transfer, and m_r is the reduced mass of the WIMP and the nucleus, m_r = \frac{m_\chi m_N}{m_\chi + m_N}. The formula is written in units where constants such as c are absorbed. Each factor collects what one community would need to know: particle theorists predict \sigma_0 and m_\chi, nuclear physicists the shape of the nucleus, and astrophysicists the density and speeds of the halo.

The astrophysics factor
The velocity distribution of the halo enters through T(E_R) = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\,v_0\int_{v_{\min}}^{\infty}\frac{f_1(v)}{v}\,dv, an integral over the local distribution f_1(v) of WIMP speeds, where v_0 is the characteristic speed of the halo (about 220 km/s). The lower limit is the slowest WIMP that can produce a recoil of energy E_R: v_{\min} = \sqrt{\frac{E_R\,m_N}{2m_r^2}}. For a pure Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution of speeds, the integral gives T(E_R) \simeq \exp(-v_{\min}^2/v_0^2).
Since v_{\min}^2 \propto E_R, this factor falls exponentially with recoil energy. This is the origin of the featureless, falling spectrum we will meet below: a large recoil needs a fast WIMP, and fast WIMPs are rare.


The nuclear structure factor
A WIMP scatters from the nucleus as a whole only if the momentum it transfers, q = \sqrt{2 m_N E_R}, is small enough that it cannot resolve the nucleus’s internal structure. At larger q, the waves scattered from different parts of the nucleus begin to cancel, and the form factor F(E_R) drops below 1. The slides use the Helm form factor, an approximation to a Woods–Saxon nuclear density: F^2(E_R) = \left[\frac{3\,j_1(qR_1)}{qR_1}\right]^2 e^{-(qs)^2}, where R_1 is an effective nuclear radius, s is the nuclear skin thickness (the distance over which the nuclear density falls to zero, a gradual fall rather than a step), and j_1 is the spherical Bessel function of order one. The slides label the expression F(E_R) and describe J_1 as the cylindrical Bessel function. The expression as written is F^2, and the Helm form uses the spherical function j_1.
The form factor matters most for heavy nuclei, which are large and so are resolved at smaller q.


The particle physics factor
In the simplest case, a spin-independent interaction, the WIMP couples to protons with strength f_p and to neutrons with f_n. At zero momentum transfer the amplitudes from all the nucleons in the nucleus add coherently, so \sigma_0 = \frac{4m_r^2}{\pi}\big[Z f_p + (A-Z) f_n\big]^2 \simeq \frac{4m_r^2}{\pi}\,f^2A^2, where Z is the proton number, A is the mass number (the slides call it the atomic mass), and the last form assumes f_p = f_n = f. The slides’ approximate form writes f A^2; with equal couplings the square applies to f as well.
The factor A^2 is the coherence: a nucleus of A nucleons scatters A^2 times as strongly as a single nucleon, not A times. The slides call this an enormous enhancement for heavy targets.
crumbs: 5  Week 4: Rare Event Searches and Cryogenics

title: Week 4: Rare Event Searches and Cryogenics
text:
Different targets
Which target material should we use?
The slides plot dR/dE_R for a 100 GeV/c^2 WIMP with \sigma = 10^{-45} cm² in xenon, germanium, argon, silicon and neon. At zero recoil energy the curves are ordered by mass number, and at higher energies xenon falls fastest.






Note



Worked example. Near E_R = 0 the form factor is 1 and T(0) is the same for every target, so the rate per kilogram scales as \sigma_0/m_r^2 \propto A^2. The ratio of xenon (A \approx 131) to germanium (A \approx 72.6) should then be \left(\frac{131}{72.6}\right)^2 \approx 3.3. Reading the slide’s plot, the xenon curve starts near 0.18 and germanium near 0.055 (in counts per 10 kg per keV per year), a ratio of about 3.3. The same scaling places argon (A \approx 40) near 0.055\times(40/72.6)^2 \approx 0.017, which matches its curve as well.


Xenon’s steeper fall is the form factor of the previous section: a large nucleus is resolved at lower momentum transfer.
The lecture adds a further reason to use more than one target. More general WIMP-nucleon interactions exist than the spin-independent case, and they change not only the relative rates between targets but the shapes of the spectra. The slides show two such models in which fluorine or germanium is enhanced instead of xenon. If a signal is ever seen, a programme of several target materials will be needed to work out which interaction produced it.
crumbs: 5  Week 4: Rare Event Searches and Cryogenics

title: Week 4: Rare Event Searches and Cryogenics
text:
Exposure and threshold
The slides then start a list of requirements for an ideal nuclear-recoil detector. The first two are:

Large exposure (mass times time), because the rate per kilogram per year is so small.
Low energy threshold, because the spectrum is largest at the lowest recoil energies.


Definition. The energy threshold of a detector is the smallest deposited energy it can reliably record. Events below it are lost.

Why does the threshold matter so much for light WIMPs? In an elastic collision, the most energy the WIMP can give the nucleus is in a head-on collision, which transfers momentum q_{\max} = 2m_r v. The recoil energy is then q^2/2m_N, so E_{R,\max} = \frac{2m_r^2 v^2}{m_N}. This is the slides’ \Delta E \lesssim 2M_{DM}^2v^2/M_N in the limit m_\chi \ll m_N, where m_r \approx m_\chi. Turned around, it gives the v_{\min} of the astrophysics factor: a WIMP must have at least a minimum velocity to produce a recoil of a given energy.






Note



Worked example. Take a germanium nucleus, m_N \approx 72.6\ \text{u} \approx 67.6 GeV/c^2, and a WIMP at v = 220 km/s, so \beta = v/c \approx 7.3\times10^{-4} and \beta^2 \approx 5.4\times10^{-7}. With masses in GeV/c^2, E_{R,\max} = 2(m_rc^2)^2\beta^2/(m_Nc^2).
For m_\chi = 100 GeV/c^2: m_r = (100)(67.6)/167.6 \approx 40.3 GeV/c^2, and E_{R,\max} \approx \frac{2(40.3)^2(5.4\times10^{-7})}{67.6}\ \text{GeV} \approx 2.6\times10^{-5}\ \text{GeV} = 26\ \text{keV}. For m_\chi = 5 GeV/c^2: m_r = (5)(67.6)/72.6 \approx 4.66 GeV/c^2, and E_{R,\max} \approx \frac{2(4.66)^2(5.4\times10^{-7})}{67.6}\ \text{GeV} \approx 3.5\times10^{-7}\ \text{GeV} \approx 0.35\ \text{keV}. A 100 GeV WIMP at a typical speed can leave a few tens of keV, which is the “few 10s of keV” on the slides. A 5 GeV WIMP leaves at most a few hundred eV. Only the fastest WIMPs in the tail of the distribution, several times faster than 220 km/s, can push it to a few keV.


The slides’ threshold plots show the consequence. For a germanium target, the total rate above threshold for WIMPs of 3 to 10 GeV falls by orders of magnitude as the threshold rises from zero to a few keV, and falls fastest for the lightest WIMPs. For a 5 GeV WIMP, lighter targets (silicon, oxygen) keep their rate to higher thresholds than heavy ones (xenon, tungsten), because a light nucleus takes a larger share of the WIMP’s energy. The summary slide later pairs the threshold requirement with good energy resolution (the Week 1 notion of how finely a detector measures energy).
